title: "Let the Boy Win His Spurs"
text:
On 26 August 1346, near the village of Crecy in northern France, the English army of King Edward III faced a much larger French army. The king's eldest son, Edward of Woodstock, later called the Black Prince, was sixteen. His father had given him nominal command of one of the three divisions, the one in the front line, surrounded by experienced knights to guide him.

The chronicler Jean Froissart tells that as the battle grew fierce, the prince's division came under heavy attack from the French and their allies. The knights around him grew worried and sent a messenger to the king, who was watching from a windmill on a hill above, asking him to send help.

According to Froissart, the king asked whether his son was dead, or struck down, or so badly wounded that he could not fight on. The messenger said no, but that he was in a hard fight. Then, said the king, go back to those who sent you and tell them not to send for me again as long as my son is alive. Let the boy win his spurs, he said, for if God wills it, I want the day and the honor to be his and those around him.

The prince's division held, and the English won a crushing victory. Froissart says that afterwards the king embraced his son and told him he had acquitted himself well, and the prince bowed low before his father.
lesson: Letting a child face real difficulty, while staying close enough to help, builds confidence no rescue can. Sometimes the best support is trusting them to finish the fight.
people: Edward III, Edward the Black Prince
caveat: Froissart wrote years later and dramatized his battle scenes, so the exact words are uncertain.
